content.title: About
content.content: Fruit croissant is a pastry that combines a classic flaky croissant dough with a fruit puree or fresh fruit filling. The dough is made from flour, butter, eggs and yeast, while the filling may include apple, cherry, strawberry or exotic fruits. The product offers a crisp, layered texture together with a bright fruit flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit croissants appeared in France in the early 1920s as a variation of the traditional croissant with seasonal fruits.
The flaky dough is created using the "turning" technique, repeatedly folding and rolling the dough with butter.
Fruit fillings are often cooked with a touch of sugar and cinnamon to enhance aroma.
In some regions the croissant‑fruit is finished with a light dusting of powdered sugar or a glaze.
Vegan versions replace butter with plant‑based margarine and eggs with a vegan binder.

items.title: Source of vitamins
items.content: The fruit filling provides vitamin C, vitamin A and B‑vitamins, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fruits add dietary fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in trans‑fats
items.content: When prepared correctly, the flaky dough contains minimal trans‑fats, which is better for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruits are rich in antioxidants (polyphenols, carotenoids) that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The croissant‑fruit provides quick energy from the carbohydrates in the dough and fruit.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit filling and added sugar can increase calories and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fruit acidity
items.content: Acidic fruits (e.g., cherry) may irritate the stomach lining in individuals with high acidity.

items.title: Trans‑fat formation
items.content: If baked at excessively high temperatures, trans‑fats may form, which are undesirable in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fruit croissant warm, straight from the oven. It can be enjoyed as a snack, paired with coffee or tea, or used in dessert plates together with ice cream or whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fruit croissants in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage refrigerate up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven for 5‑7 minutes before serving.
